title: 95% of what, exactly?
hook: A hundred pollsters each report a 95% interval. How many of them are wrong?

knows: that a poll reports a share plus or minus a margin of error
that random samples wobble around the truth
doesNotKnow: that "95%" describes the method over many polls, not one interval
that some intervals miss and look no different from those that hit

misconception: A 95% interval is right 95% of the time in the sense that every interval you see is trustworthy, and the misses never appear.
objective: The learner can explain that across many polls about 5 in 100 intervals miss the truth (5.4% here), and that one interval on its own gives no sign whether it is a miss.
keyState: The first batch of 100 intervals drawn, with some red bars that miss the 50% line.

claims.text: With true support exactly 50% and 1,000 random people per poll, the usual 95% interval (share +/- 1.96 x sqrt(share x (1 - share) / 1,000)) misses 50% with chance 5.4%: about 5 in 100.
claims.source: Exact binomial sum over the head counts whose interval excludes 0.5: 0.05368 (exactMiss() in src/demos/probability/ninety-five-percent-of-what/model.ts). Slightly above 5% because the interval is an approximation.

claims.text: The stage's pollsters are seeded: the first batch of 100 had 7 misses; ten batches had 7, 6, 9, 11, 11, 4, 7, 4, 6, 1 (66 of 1,000, 6.6%).
claims.source: intervals() in model.ts, mulberry32 seed 1937, untuned (the first seed tried). Over seeds 1-300 the misses in one batch of 100 had middle 95% 1-11 (median 5); 2 of 300 seeds gave 0. The reveal quotes only the learner's own counts.

claims.text: The true value is known here only because this is a simulation.
claims.source: Model setup: the population is fixed at exactly 50% support.

claims.text: The 95% belongs to the method: across many polls about 1 in 20 intervals misses, and a single interval gives no sign whether it is one of them.
claims.source: Neyman (1937), Outline of a Theory of Statistical Estimation, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 236: 333-380 (coverage as a long-run property of the procedure).

recall.question: A lab reports a 95% interval for a drug's effect. What does the 95% describe?
options: A 95% chance that this particular interval is right
How often intervals made this way catch the true value, over many studies
That 95% of patients fall inside the interval
recall.why: The 95% is a property of the method: about 19 in 20 intervals made this way contain the truth. Any one interval either does or does not, and you cannot tell which from the interval alone.
